question: A 29-year-old woman at 38 weeks gestation comes to the emergency room with regular contractions and spontaneous rupture of membranes. She subsequently delivers a 3500g (7lbs 7oz) newborn with ambiguous genitalia by spontaneous vaginal delivery. Her pregnancy and labor was uncomplicated. Examination of the newborn demonstrated no palpable gonads at the inguinal canal or perineum. Karyotype analysis demonstrated 46,XX. What is the best explanation for this patient’s presentation?

options.opb: Defective migration of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) releasing neurons
options.opd: Exposure to excessive androgenic steroids during gestation

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Ambiguous genitalia" -> "46,XX karyotype" -> "No palpable gonads" -> "Exposure to androgens in utero" -> "Excessive androgenic steroids during gestation" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Ambiguous genitalia" -> "46,XX karyotype" -> "No palpable gonads" -> "Defective androgen receptors" -> "Unlikely in 46,XX" -> 40%
CHAIN: "Ambiguous genitalia" -> "46,XX karyotype" -> "No palpable gonads" -> "Deficiency of 5-alpha-reductase" -> "Unlikely in 46,XX" -> 30%
CHAIN: "Ambiguous genitalia" -> "46,XX karyotype" -> "No palpable gonads" -> "Defective migration of GnRH neurons" -> "Unrelated to genital development" -> 20%
CHAIN: "Ambiguous genitalia" -> "46,XX karyotype" -> "No palpable gonads" -> "Ovarian dysgenesis" -> "Unlikely cause of ambiguous genitalia" -> 25%
analysis: The newborn with ambiguous genitalia and a 46,XX karyotype suggests a condition of virilization due to exposure to androgens. The absence of palpable gonads and the karyotype confirm the presence of ovaries, ruling out androgen insensitivity syndrome and 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, which are associated with 46,XY karyotype. Ovarian dysgenesis typically does not result in ambiguous genitalia. The most likely explanation is exposure to excessive androgenic steroids during gestation, which can cause virilization in a genetically female fetus.
